name: Red-Orange
lede: Red-orange is the in-between hue of the paint wheel, a name made of two plain color words, and the color most people judge as the warmest.

sections.title: Two words, one hue
sections.body:
Red-orange is a name built from two others, not a name with a story. On the twelve-color wheel used to mix paint it is one of the six tertiary colors, made by mixing a primary with the secondary next to it [1][2]. Paterson's list of the wheel's twelve places writes the same step the other way round, as orange-red, between red and orange [2]. Who first wrote it down is undocumented, and the books treat it as a plain hue name.

It sits between [[red]] and [[orange]], with [[scarlet]] and [[vermilion]] close by on the red side, and [[coral]] and [[tangerine]] on the pale side. Paterson lists "old coral" as a red-orange [3].

sections.title: Three red-oranges that do not agree
sections.body:
The swatch is bright and light, with a lightness of about 60 and a strong chroma of 77 [4]. Our sources record three different colors under the same name. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this swatch under block 11, which it calls "deep yellowish pink", 5.5 units away, so that standard does not call it red-orange at all [4]. The German RAL set, whose RAL 2001 is first recorded in our sources in 1927, is a much darker brick, about #BE4E20 on a screen, and the xkcd color survey's is a hotter #FD3C06 [4]. Each differs from the swatch by about 25 units of CIELAB distance, a gap anyone can see [4].

The lesson is that a name made of two hue words has no fixed place. The first record in our sources is RAL's, from 1927 [4].

sections.title: The warmest color
sections.body:
Birren reports a study by Newhall in which 297 observers judged 50 color samples for warmth and coolness [5]. Their "warmest" judgments clustered strongly in the red-orange region, while their "coolest" judgments were spread from yellow through green and blue to purple [5]. By this evidence red-orange is the warm color most people agree on, though the study measures judgments of warmth, not temperature [5].

Staring at a strong red or red-orange and then looking at a white surface produces an afterimage in the complementary color, a green or blue-green, as Albers describes the classroom demonstration [6]. Birren also repeats an older claim, from color therapists he puts on the wrong side of the medical profession, that red-orange pairs with indigo-blue and that colors can cure illness [7]. The claim that colors heal is a myth, and the pairing is old opinion, not evidence [7].

sections.title: Where it shows up
sections.body:
Red-orange is the glow of a sunset. Gurney notes that the boldest red-orange forms in the sky where the sun crosses the horizon, and that only the lowest clouds receive the high-chroma red-orange light as the sky dims [8]. A neon sign is a harder case: its red-orange is both very light and very saturated, which paint cannot match, so Gurney's painter used a pure tint of the hue and a flood of the same color at mid value around it [8].

In pigments, [[vermilion]] owes its red-orange to mercury [8]. The Pigment Compendium uses Red-Orange as one of its own color classes [9]. It files there burnt orpiment, a name for synthetic realgar made by heating [[orpiment]], and orange lead [10]. It also files Pliny's sandyx, a mixture of white lead and roasted red ochre [10]. The hematite-rich Red Chalk at Hunstanton in Norfolk is described there as a strong red-orange [9]. In gems, spessartine is the red-orange member of the [[gem:garnet|garnet]] family [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Only 6 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive hold this color, within six units of the swatch and covering at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [12]. Five of the six are from the 1600s, about 3 times the expected rate, and 4 are Indian, about 22 times the rate for India's 721 paintings [12]. The Rajput school accounts for 2 of its 97 paintings, 82 times the expected rate [12]. These are look-alikes in photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not proof of a pigment [12].

The strongest case is a 1611 [[painting:cma-314494|portrait of Prince Sur Singh Rathor of Bikaner]], where the color covers 61 per cent of the picture [12]. A smaller share, 16 per cent, is in a Rajput scene of [[painting:cma-314489|Rati taking aim at Krishna]], and 18 per cent in [[painting:commons-Q19968967|The Pale Complexion of True Love]], painted in 1899 by Eleanor Fortescue-Brickdale [12]. Rajput court painting is the place to look for it, in large areas [12].
